title: Sulfonylurea (glipizide) hypoglycemia: targets membrane K-ATP channels
vignette: A 46-year-old woman comes to the office due to frequent episodes of headache, nausea, sweating, and a feeling as if she is going to pass out. The patient has had 3 such episodes in the past 2 weeks, with symptoms occurring when she skips a meal. During the most recent episode, finger-stick glucose was 50 mg/dL. She was diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus 3 years ago and initially treated with metformin monotherapy; glipizide was added 3 months ago due to inadequate glycemic control. The patient has no other medical conditions. Vital signs are within normal limits and physical examination shows no abnormalities. Hemoglobin A1c is 6.9%. The medication most likely responsible for this patient's current symptoms works by targeting which of the following?

clues.text: symptoms occurring when she skips a meal
clues.note: Adrenergic symptoms triggered by skipping a meal indicate drug-induced hypoglycemia from an insulin secretagogue.
Documented hypoglycemia (50 mg/dL) confirms the episodes are due to excess insulin secretion.
Glipizide is a SULFONYLUREA (insulin secretagogue) - the cause of hypoglycemia; it acts on pancreatic beta-cell K-ATP channels.

whatMatters: Hypoglycemia after skipping meals in a patient on GLIPIZIDE = sulfonylurea effect. Sulfonylureas close the ATP-sensitive POTASSIUM (K-ATP) CHANNELS on the beta-cell MEMBRANE, depolarizing the cell to trigger glucose-INDEPENDENT insulin release. So the drug targets MEMBRANE ION CHANNELS. Answer C.
strategy: Identify the culprit (glipizide, a sulfonylurea) and recall its target: the beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ channel (a membrane ion channel). Closing it depolarizes the cell -> Ca2+ influx -> insulin release regardless of glucose -> hypoglycemia. Reject metformin's target (mitochondrial enzymes/AMPK - no hypoglycemia), TZD (nuclear PPAR-gamma receptors), GLP-1/incretin (surface adenylate-cyclase-coupled receptors), and insulin's receptor (surface tyrosine kinase).

eliminations.label: Intracellular mitochondrial enzymes - metformin (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: metformin inhibits mitochondrial enzymes of gluconeogenesis and activates AMPK. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: metformin does not increase insulin secretion and rarely causes hypoglycemia; the meal-skipping hypoglycemia is due to the sulfonylurea (K-ATP channel). ✅ Correct if: asking about metformin's mechanism.

eliminations.label: Intracellular nuclear receptors - thiazolidinediones
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: TZDs (pioglitazone) activate the nuclear transcription factor PPAR-gamma. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that's a different class that improves insulin sensitivity, not the K-ATP-channel secretagogue causing hypoglycemia. ✅ Correct if: a TZD mechanism question.

eliminations.label: Surface adenylate cyclase-coupled receptors - GLP-1 agonists
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: GLP-1 receptor agonists act through G-protein/adenylate-cyclase-coupled surface receptors (glucose-dependent). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: those cause glucose-dependent insulin release with low hypoglycemia risk - not the culprit. ✅ Correct if: an incretin/GLP-1 mechanism.

eliminations.label: Surface tyrosine kinase receptor - insulin receptor
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: the insulin receptor (a surface receptor tyrosine kinase). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: that's the receptor for insulin itself, not the target of sulfonylureas. ✅ Correct if: describing insulin's own receptor.

reasoning: Meal-skipping hypoglycemia in a patient on glipizide = sulfonylurea effect
Sulfonylureas bind and CLOSE the ATP-sensitive potassium (K-ATP) channel on the beta-cell membrane
Membrane depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels -> insulin release (glucose-independent)
-> the drug targets membrane ion channels; answer C
mechanism: Glipizide is a SULFONYLUREA, an insulin secretagogue. It binds the SUR1 subunit of the ATP-sensitive POTASSIUM (K-ATP) CHANNEL on the pancreatic beta-cell MEMBRANE and CLOSES it. Normally these channels close only when intracellular ATP rises (i.e., when glucose is high); by closing them pharmacologically, sulfonylureas DEPOLARIZE the beta-cell membrane, opening voltage-gated CALCIUM channels so calcium influx triggers insulin EXOCYTOSIS - crucially, INDEPENDENT of the blood glucose level. This glucose-independent insulin release is why sulfonylureas can cause HYPOGLYCEMIA, especially when a meal is skipped (no incoming glucose) or with renal/hepatic impairment or longer-acting agents. Therefore the drug's target is a MEMBRANE ION CHANNEL (the K-ATP channel). The distractors are the targets of other agents: metformin (intracellular mitochondrial enzymes/AMPK), thiazolidinediones (nuclear PPAR-gamma), GLP-1 agonists (surface adenylate-cyclase-coupled receptors), and insulin (surface receptor tyrosine kinase).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Pharm > sulfonylureas: close beta-cell K-ATP (SUR1) channel -> depolarization -> Ca2+ influx -> glucose-independent insulin release -> hypoglycemia; contrast metformin (mitochondrial/AMPK), TZD (PPAR-gamma), GLP-1 (surface GPCR).

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Glipizide (sulfonylurea) targets the beta-cell K-ATP channel = membrane ion channel.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on sulfonylurea, K-ATP channel/SUR1, insulin secretagogue, or glucose-independent insulin release? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Mitochondrial enzymes = metformin; nuclear receptors = TZD; adenylate-cyclase GPCR = GLP-1; tyrosine kinase = insulin receptor.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: sulfonylureas close beta-cell K-ATP channel (membrane ion channel) -> insulin release; hypoglycemia risk (skipped meals, CKD, glyburide).

keywords.back: Beta-cell ATP-sensitive K+ (K-ATP) channel (membrane ion channel)
Close K-ATP -> depolarize -> Ca2+ influx -> insulin release (glucose-independent)
Insulin secretion independent of blood glucose

firstAid.detail: Pharm: close beta-cell K-ATP channel (membrane ion channel) -> insulin release.
Pharm > metformin (mitochondria), TZD (nuclear), GLP-1 (GPCR), insulin (tyrosine kinase).
Pharm > worse with skipped meals, renal/hepatic disease, glyburide.

memoryHook: Glipizide slams the beta cell's potassium door (K-ATP channel) shut - the cell depolarizes and dumps insulin no matter the sugar, so skipping a meal tanks the glucose.
